title: Batman's Treaty
subtitle: The Port Phillip deeds, the Kulin ngurungaeta and the Crown, 1835–1837
intro: On 6 June 1835, beside a creek north of the Yarra River, John Batman handed blankets, knives, tomahawks and flour to a group of Kulin men and came away with two documents. They declared that eight ngurungaeta (headmen), three of them written down as 'Jagajaga', had granted about 600,000 acres around Port Phillip to him and his partners in return for those goods and a yearly 'rent or tribute'. It is the only documented attempt by colonists to make a treaty with Aboriginal people for their land in Australia. Within three months the Governor of New South Wales had declared it void.

The record is lopsided, and this chapter says so plainly. Almost every word about the meeting comes from Batman himself: his journal, his deeds and his report to Governor Arthur. No Wurundjeri (Woiwurrung) or Boonwurrung (Bunurong) record from 1835 survives, and no one at the creek could translate between Woiwurrung and English; Batman's interpreters were Aboriginal men from the Sydney district who spoke another language. The ngurungaeta appear here as an eye made only of what the other side wrote down. William Barak, who said he watched as a boy, speaks only through memory recorded long afterward.

What the elders understood is set out as positions, not settled. The deed reads as a grant of land. Historians such as Bain Attwood and Eva Bischoff, and Wurundjeri people today, point to tanderrum, the Kulin ceremony that welcomes visitors and gives them temporary access to Country in return for reciprocal obligations, as the likelier meaning of soil and gifts passing hand to hand. Gareth Knapman reads the deed's own legal form, drafted in Hobart by Joseph Gellibrand, as a feudal grant binding the grantees to a continuing tribute. William Buckley, the escaped convict who had lived with the Wadawurrung (Wathaurong) for thirty-two years, said in 1852 that no chief held a right over the soil that could be sold.

Around the deed the record widens into letters and official papers: the camp journal of William Todd, left to hold the claim; the reports of the surveyor J. H. Wedge; the journal of John Pascoe Fawkner, whose rival party ignored the deed; Gellibrand's memoranda of a visit in 1836; and the despatches of Governors Arthur and Bourke and of Lord Glenelg in London. Bourke's proclamation of 26 August 1835 and Glenelg's approval of April 1836 settled the colonial law: the Crown alone could acquire land from Aboriginal people, and it treated the land as already its own.

The epilogue is Melbourne. In March 1837 Bourke came to Port Phillip, approved the town plan and named the village on the Yarra; on 1 June 1837 the Crown sold the first town lots. The Association went on delivering tribute goods for a time, then stopped. The dates below let the purchaser, the people on the bank, the camp-keeper, the interpreter, the rival and the governors be read against one another, week by week.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Batman's journal and his report to Arthur disagree slightly: the journal has the Rebecca leaving Launceston on Sunday 10 May and entering Port Phillip on Friday 29 May 1835, while the report gives 12 May and 26 May; the journal's weekdays match the calendar, so its dates are used, and the 12 May date probably marks clearing the Tamar. Sources also differ on Buckley's arrival at the Indented Head camp (usually 6 July; Wedge gives 12 July) and on Fawkner's own arrival on the Yarra (10 or 16 October 1835); those entries are marked approximate.

eyes.name: John Batman
eyes.role: Van Diemen's Land grazier, aged 34, agent of the Port Phillip Association
eyes.side: Port Phillip Association (Launceston and Hobart investors)
eyes.where: On the schooner Rebecca and on foot from Indented Head to the Merri Creek and the Yarra

waypoints.label: Hobart Town, report to Arthur, 25 June

eyes.vantage_label: the purchaser, author of the deeds' story
eyes.authenticity: The manuscript journal (10 May–11 June 1835) is State Library Victoria MS 13181; it passed through the family of his son-in-law William Weire. It was first printed in 1856 and again by James Bonwick (in fragments in 1867, more fully in 1883). It is the only near-contemporary account of the 6 June meeting. Squiggled marks on one journal page resemble the 'signatures' on the deeds, which has led some historians to suspect Batman drew the marks himself. His official report to Governor Arthur (25 June 1835) differs from the journal in some dates (12 May sailing, 26 May landing).
eyes.bio: Born at Parramatta, New South Wales, Batman had taken part in the violence of the 'Black War' in Van Diemen's Land and also in G. A. Robinson's conciliation efforts. In 1835 he crossed Bass Strait with seven Aboriginal men from the Sydney district and came back with two deeds claiming about 600,000 acres. His journal is the record on which almost everything said about the 'treaty' depends.

sources.title: John Batman, Journal 10 May – 11 June 1835, MS 13181, State Library Victoria
James Bonwick, John Batman, the Founder of Victoria (Melbourne, 1867), Project Gutenberg Australia
F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia

eyes.name: The eight ngurungaeta named in the deeds (Jagajaga brothers, Cooloolock, Bungarie, Yanyan, Moowhip, Mommarmalar)
eyes.role: Ngurungaeta (headmen) of Kulin clans; later historians identify among them the Wurundjeri brothers Bebejan and Billibellary
eyes.side: Kulin nation: Wurundjeri (Woiwurrung) and Boonwurrung (Bunurong) clans
eyes.where: A creek north of the Yarra, usually identified as the Merri Creek; the exact site is disputed
eyes.vantage_label: the other party, recorded only by the purchaser
eyes.form: marks on a deed and actions as recorded by the other side
eyes.authenticity: No Wurundjeri record from 1835 survives. Their names, marks and actions exist only in Batman's journal, his deeds and his report, written in English. No trained interpreter was present: Batman relied on his Sydney-district Aboriginal companions, whose language differed from Woiwurrung. Batman wrote three principal chiefs as 'Jagajaga' (Jika Jika); of the eight, four have been identified with confidence by later historians, among them Bebejan and Billibellary. Whether the uniform marks were made by the men themselves is questioned.
eyes.bio: The ngurungaeta were senior men who spoke for their clans' Country. What they understood on 6 June is the central open question: a sale of land, as the deed reads, or a tanderrum, the Kulin ceremony that grants visitors temporary access to Country with obligations of reciprocity. They are included here as the party whose record is missing, with their actions given only as Batman set them down.

sources.title: Eva Bischoff, 'An Elm Tree at the Yarra River? Batman's Treaty as a Nexus of Settler-Colonial Space|Time', Comparativ 33/1 (2023)
Bain Attwood, 'Batman's treaty', eMelbourne (Encyclopedia of Melbourne)
Shane Carmody, 'John Batman's Place in the Village', La Trobe Journal 80 (2007)

eyes.name: William Barak (Beruk)
eyes.role: Wurundjeri boy of about eleven or twelve in 1835; son of Bebejan; later ngurungaeta at Coranderrk
eyes.where: Present as a child at the 1835 meeting, by his own later account
eyes.authenticity: Barak's recollection that he and his cousin Wonga watched the 'signing' survives only in later reports and in reflections taken down by others in his old age; the date on which this particular memory was first recorded has not been established here. Historians note his claim but cannot confirm it. He insisted the meeting took place at a different creek from the one usually named.
eyes.bio: Barak became the best-known Wurundjeri leader of the later nineteenth century, a painter and advocate for the Coranderrk community. He is the one Kulin voice who claimed to have seen the 1835 meeting, which makes his recollection precious and, as memory, hard to test.

sources.title: Bain Attwood, 'Batman's treaty', eMelbourne (Encyclopedia of Melbourne)
History of St Albans: William Barak (compiled 2025)

eyes.name: William Todd (Andrew alias William Todd)
eyes.role: Batman's employee and recorder, one of three white men left at Indented Head
eyes.where: The camp at Indented Head on the Bellarine Peninsula
eyes.authenticity: Manuscript journal, 8 June–15 November 1835, State Library Victoria MS 11243. Published in an annotated edition, 'Andrew alias William Todd (John Batman's recorder) and his Indented Head journal 1835', edited by Philip L. Brown. It is the only daily record kept on the claimed land in the weeks after Batman left.
eyes.bio: Todd was left at Indented Head with James Gumm, Alexander Thomson and five Sydney Aboriginal men to hold the claim. His journal records the day-to-day contact with Wadawurrung (Wathaurong) people and the sudden appearance of William Buckley.

sources.title: William Todd's journal: Buckley's tattoo (State Library Victoria, image study)
The Todd journal, 1835 (Deakin University Library record)

eyes.name: William Buckley
eyes.role: Escaped convict, aged about 55, who had lived with the Wadawurrung (Wathaurong) for some 32 years
eyes.side: Between worlds: a Wadawurrung kinsman by adoption, then interpreter for the colonists
eyes.where: The Bellarine Peninsula; then Batman's settlement on the Yarra

waypoints.label: walks into the Indented Head camp, July 1835

eyes.vantage_label: the only European who knew Kulin law from within
eyes.form: memoir (written later, as told to John Morgan)
eyes.authenticity: The Life and Adventures of William Buckley was published at Hobart in 1852, written by John Morgan from Buckley's telling, seventeen years after the events; Morgan's shaping and errors of date (he gives 21 August for the pardon, actually dated 28 August 1835) are acknowledged. Contemporary journals (Todd, Wedge, Gellibrand) confirm his arrival and his role as interpreter.
eyes.bio: Buckley escaped from the 1803 Sullivan Bay settlement and was taken in by Wadawurrung people. His reappearance gave the Association an interpreter. Speaking through Morgan in 1852, he denied that any chief held a right over the soil that he could sell, a position set here beside the deed's text.

sources.title: Buckley's return to European life (State Library Victoria)
Batman's treaty (State Library Victoria, ergo)
F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia

eyes.name: John Helder Wedge
eyes.role: Surveyor and member of the Port Phillip Association, aged 42
eyes.where: Van Diemen's Land, then Port Phillip from 7 August 1835

waypoints.label: Kingston (Batman's farm), maps the claim, 14–15 June

eyes.vantage_label: the Association's surveyor in the district
eyes.authenticity: Wedge's 'Description of the Country around Port Phillip' and narrative of his excursion were forwarded by Arthur to London on 28 January 1836 and printed in parliamentary papers; Labilliere (1878) reprints them. His map of Batman's route and the claimed boundaries, drawn at Kingston on 14–15 June 1835, was ordered printed by the House of Commons on 1 August 1836.
eyes.bio: Wedge turned Batman's compass-and-estimate journey into the map that went to London with the deeds. He then went to Port Phillip himself, met Buckley, and urged his pardon.

sources.title: F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia
A. H. Campbell and J. Scurfield, 'An Historic Chart of Batman's Exploration', La Trobe Journal 36 (1985)

eyes.name: John Pascoe Fawkner
eyes.role: Launceston publican and newspaper owner, aged 43, organiser of the rival Enterprize party
eyes.side: Independent settlers outside the Port Phillip Association
eyes.where: Launceston, then the Yarra settlement from October 1835
eyes.vantage_label: rival settler who rejected the treaty
eyes.authenticity: 'Journal of preparations for departure to and proceedings at Port Phillip', 18 July 1835 – 8 August 1836, National Library of Australia MS 3224 (Ferguson collection); published as Melbourne's Missing Chronicle, ed. C. P. Billot (Melbourne, 1982). Because the edition is modern, no quotation is used.
eyes.bio: Fawkner had been a boy at the 1803 Sullivan Bay settlement, like Buckley. His party reached the Yarra in late August 1835 without him; he followed in October. He treated Batman's deed as worthless and spent the rest of his life contesting Batman's title as founder.

sources.title: Pam Ray, 'Manuscripts in the National Library of Australia Relating to the Settlement of Port Phillip', La Trobe Journal 34 (1984)
F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia

eyes.name: Joseph Tice Gellibrand
eyes.role: Hobart barrister, former Attorney-General of Van Diemen's Land, aged about 43; drafted the deed
eyes.where: Hobart; at Port Phillip 25 January – 16 February 1836
eyes.vantage_label: the deed's lawyer, visiting the ground
eyes.form: diary (memoranda of a journey); legal instruments
eyes.authenticity: His memoranda were sent to Governor Bourke under a covering letter of 18 April 1836, marked as not an official document. The manuscript was damaged by fire at the printers in 1858; it was read to the Philosophical Institute of Victoria on 8 September 1858 and reported in The Argus next day, with illegible words marked by the editor.
eyes.bio: Gellibrand wrote the pro-forma deed modelled on an English feoffment, with a yearly 'rent or tribute'. In early 1836 he went to see the land and its people, used Buckley as interpreter, and dealt with an assault by a shepherd on an Aboriginal woman. He disappeared in the Port Phillip district in 1837.

sources.title: Mr J. T. Gellibrand's Memoranda of a Trip to Port Phillip in 1836, Geelong Historical Society
Bain Attwood, 'Batman's treaty', eMelbourne (Encyclopedia of Melbourne)

eyes.name: Sir George Arthur
eyes.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Van Diemen's Land, aged 50
eyes.authenticity: Official correspondence of the Van Diemen's Land government; his letters on treaties, on Buckley's pardon and on forwarding Wedge's report are cited by Bischoff (2023) and Labilliere (1878).
eyes.bio: Arthur had presided over the 'Black War' and the removal of Tasmanian Aboriginal people. Early in 1835 he wrote that failing to make a treaty at first settlement had been a great error, and the deeds and Wedge's chart were sent on to him, though the land lay outside his jurisdiction.

sources.title: Eva Bischoff, 'An Elm Tree at the Yarra River? Batman's Treaty as a Nexus of Settler-Colonial Space|Time', Comparativ 33/1 (2023)
F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia

eyes.name: Sir Richard Bourke
eyes.role: Governor of New South Wales, aged 57
eyes.where: Government House, Sydney; Port Phillip in March 1837
eyes.vantage_label: the governor who voided the deeds
eyes.authenticity: The proclamation of 26 August 1835 and his despatch to Glenelg of 10 October 1835 are official documents printed in parliamentary papers and reprinted by Labilliere (1878); the copy sent to London is held in the UK National Archives (Documenting a Democracy).
eyes.bio: An Irish-born liberal Whig, Bourke had no wish to see colonists treat with Aboriginal people as landholders, because it would deny the Crown's title. His proclamation declared such bargains void and the settlers trespassers; within two years he was laying out Melbourne himself.

sources.title: F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia
Governor Bourke's Proclamation 1835 (Documenting a Democracy, Museum of Australian Democracy)

eyes.name: Charles Grant, Lord Glenelg
eyes.role: Secretary of State for War and the Colonies, aged 57
eyes.authenticity: His despatch to Bourke of 13 April 1836 is printed in parliamentary papers and reprinted by Labilliere (1878).
eyes.bio: An evangelical humanitarian in office while the House of Commons Select Committee on Aborigines sat (1835–37), Glenelg upheld Bourke: the Crown alone could acquire land from Aboriginal people.

sources.title: F. P. Labilliere, Early History of the Colony of Victoria, vol. II (London, 1878), Project Gutenberg Australia
Eva Bischoff, 'An Elm Tree at the Yarra River? Batman's Treaty as a Nexus of Settler-Colonial Space|Time', Comparativ 33/1 (2023)

entries.headline: Arthur writes that a treaty should have been made at first
entries.digest: Months before Batman sailed, Arthur wrote that it had been a great oversight not to make a treaty with the Aboriginal people when Van Diemen's Land was first occupied. He urged that any further land be acquired by treaty before settlers moved in. The Association later leaned on this view.
entries.source_note: Bischoff 2023, citing Arthur's letter of 27 January 1835

entries.headline: Rebecca sails with Sydney men aboard
entries.digest: Batman left Launceston in the small schooner Rebecca with servants and seven Aboriginal men from the Sydney district, among them Pigeon, Bungett and Joe. Contrary winds held the vessel in the Tamar. His later report to Arthur gives 12 May as the sailing date.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 10 May, as printed by Bonwick (1867); SLV catalogue dates the journal from 10 May; Labilliere for the letter's 12 May

entries.place: Port Sorell, northern Van Diemen's Land
entries.headline: Gale drives the Rebecca into Port Sorell
entries.digest: A northerly gale forced the Rebecca to shelter in Port Sorell, the little vessel pitching hard. Batman's entries in these days fret about the delay and about his wife Eliza, left behind at George Town.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 19–20 May, as printed by Bonwick (1867)

entries.place: Port Phillip Heads and Indented Head
entries.headline: Through the Heads into a great bay
entries.digest: After nineteen days the Rebecca entered Port Phillip. Batman admired the harbour as the finest basin of water he had seen and landed at Indented Head, where a dog was howling on the shore. The official report to Arthur gives the landing as 26 May.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 29 May (Bonwick 1867); SLV timeline: entered Port Phillip on the 29th

entries.headline: A grazier's eye on the Geelong plains
entries.digest: Batman walked about twenty miles and looked over the open plains toward Geelong. He judged the land excellent for sheep and noted that good hay could be made there: the journal reads the country as pasture first.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 30 May (Bonwick 1867)

entries.headline: Women and children meet the party
entries.digest: Following tracks, Batman's men came on about twenty women and twenty-four children. The women sang and danced, and he handed out handkerchiefs, beads, looking-glasses, sugar and apples. It was the expedition's first sustained meeting with Kulin people; the men were away.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 31 May (Bonwick 1867)

entries.headline: The recorder's camp begins
entries.digest: Todd's journal opens as Batman's boat leaves, and records the small party building shelter and trading with Wadawurrung (Wathaurong) people who came to the camp. The entries are plain and practical: food, weather, visitors.
entries.source_note: Todd journal, 8 June–15 November 1835 (SLV MS 11243; SLV ergo)

entries.place: Plains west of the Saltwater (Maribyrnong) River
entries.headline: Naming hills for the investors
entries.digest: Moving north and east across the volcanic plains, Batman named Mount Wedge and other features after Association members and called the pasture the most beautiful he had ever seen. The naming ran ahead of any agreement with the people whose Country it was.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 4 June (Bonwick 1867)

entries.place: A creek north of the Yarra, usually identified as the Merri Creek
entries.headline: Gifts, marks and handfuls of soil
entries.digest: Batman met a man with his wife and children and gave them blankets, handkerchiefs, beads and knives; eight armed men then came up, laid down their spears and shook hands. By his account the terms were agreed by speech and gesture, the goods handed over, and in the afternoon the men he called chiefs made their marks on his deeds and each handed him a piece of soil, which he took as giving him full possession. He named a creek after himself.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 6 June (Bonwick 1867; Bischoff 2023); deed dated 6 June 1835 (SLV)

entries.headline: What the record shows the ngurungaeta doing
entries.digest: In Batman's record the eight men lay down their weapons, accept the goods, mark the deeds, hand over soil and give in return weapons and two possum-skin cloaks, which Batman called royal mantles. Their own words were not written down, and no shared language was available to explain a sale. Later historians read the exchange of soil and gifts as close to tanderrum, the Kulin rite that admits visitors to Country on terms; the deed reads it as a grant of land.
entries.source_note: Batman journal and deeds as discussed by Bischoff 2023 and Attwood (eMelbourne)

entries.place: The 1835 meeting place, as he remembered it
entries.headline: A boy watches the strangers' paper
entries.digest: Barak, about eleven, later said that he and his cousin Wonga had watched the meeting at which marks were put on Batman's paper. In old age he was firm that it happened at a different creek from the one historians usually name. The recollection survives in later reports, not in a record from 1835.
entries.source_note: Attwood (eMelbourne) notes Barak's claim; History of St Albans compilation (2025) on the location; recording date not established

entries.place: The Yarra River, near the later Flinders Street
entries.headline: The place for a village
entries.digest: Rowing up the Yarra, Batman found deep fresh water above the falls and marked the spot in his journal as the site for a settlement, with people on the bank watching. The line became Melbourne's founding phrase; the city's official founding date was later set by Fawkner's party instead.
entries.quote: This will be the place for a village
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 8 June (SLV MS 13181; Carmody, La Trobe Journal 80)

entries.headline: Leaving men to hold the claim
entries.digest: Batman landed his stores at Indented Head and left William Todd, James Gumm, Alexander Thomson and five Sydney men with seed, fruit and dogs. He gave Gumm written authority to remove trespassers, a claim of private control over land the Crown would shortly deny he could hold.
entries.source_note: Batman journal, 9 June (Bonwick 1867)

entries.place: Kingston, Batman's farm, Van Diemen's Land
entries.headline: The claim becomes a map
entries.digest: Back across Bass Strait, Batman sat with Wedge at Kingston and Wedge drew a chart of the route and the boundaries of the two tracts. Batman had fixed positions only by compass and estimated distances, so the lines on the map were broad guesses. The chart went to Arthur with the deeds.
entries.source_note: Campbell and Scurfield, La Trobe Journal 36 (1985)

entries.headline: Report to the Lieutenant-Governor
entries.digest: Batman reported to Arthur that he had bought about 600,000 acres from the chiefs, described the country as decidedly superior to any he had seen, and told how the chiefs marked trees at the boundaries and handed him soil. He said he had left Port Phillip on 14 June. He enclosed the deeds and asked for Crown recognition.
entries.source_note: Batman to Arthur, 25 June 1835, in Labilliere (1878); Campbell and Scurfield (1985) on forwarding

entries.headline: The deeds pass to the Association's trustees
entries.digest: An indenture of 29 June set out how Batman and the Van Diemen's Land investors would share the land, and on 30 June Batman conveyed both tracts to Swanston, Gellibrand and Simpson in trust. The legal paperwork in Hobart moved faster than any further contact at Port Phillip.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878), indenture and conveyance

entries.headline: A giant walks into camp
entries.digest: Todd wrote that a very tall man in skins came in, ate heartily and said he was William Buckley, showing the initials W. B. on his arm. Gumm measured him at around six feet seven, and Todd noted that he had nearly lost his English but spoke the local language fluently. The party clothed him and shared their rations.
entries.source_note: Todd journal (SLV ergo transcript excerpt); the entry's day is usually given as 6 July, Wedge gives 12 July

entries.headline: Buckley's own account of coming in
entries.digest: Buckley later said he heard of the strangers from his Wadawurrung kin and went to the camp uncertain whether he would be taken as an escaped convict. In the 1852 Life he also dismissed the idea that the people had sold their land, saying they had no chiefs with any superior right over the soil.
entries.quote: no chiefs claiming or possessing any superior right over the soil
entries.source_note: Morgan, Life and Adventures of William Buckley (Hobart 1852), as quoted by SLV ergo

entries.headline: The rival journal opens
entries.digest: Fawkner began a journal of his preparations to send a party to Port Phillip in the Enterprize, which he had bought for the venture. Its opening entries are about stores, men and money, not about the Association's deed.
entries.source_note: Fawkner journal, 18 July 1835 – 8 August 1836 (NLA MS 3224; Ray, La Trobe Journal 34)

entries.headline: Wedge tells Fawkner's men of the treaty
entries.digest: Wedge came on the Enterprize party on the Yarra and told them that the land had been bought from the chiefs. They took no notice, and Fawkner afterwards dismissed the deed as worthless.
entries.source_note: Secondary summary of Batman's Treaty (cavac mirror of Wikipedia); Labilliere (1878) on the Enterprize

entries.headline: The surveyor lands
entries.digest: Wedge landed at Port Phillip to inspect the claim and met Buckley at the Indented Head camp. His narrative described open, grassy country and its people, and he wrote urging a pardon for Buckley so that he could serve as interpreter.
entries.source_note: Wedge's narrative of his excursion, in Labilliere (1878)

entries.headline: Proclamation: the bargain is void
entries.digest: Bourke proclaimed that any treaty, bargain or contract with Aboriginal people for land was void against the rights of the Crown, and that anyone occupying vacant Crown land without authority was a trespasser. The deeds were not named but were plainly the target. The proclamation rested on the view that the Crown already owned the land.
entries.source_note: Proclamation of 26 August 1835 in Labilliere (1878); Documenting a Democracy

entries.headline: A pardon for Buckley
entries.digest: Arthur signed a free pardon for William Buckley, thirty-two years after his escape. Buckley's language and kinship made him useful as an interpreter, and Wedge's letter had argued exactly that.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878): pardon dated 28 August 1835 (Morgan gives 21 August)

entries.headline: Fawkner's party moors on the Yarra
entries.digest: Fawkner's men landed on 29 August and moored the Enterprize near the later Custom House site on 30 August. Fawkner himself was still in Launceston. The 30 August date later became Melbourne's official founding day.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878); Carmody (2007) on the official founding date

entries.headline: Fawkner arrives at his own settlement
entries.digest: Fawkner reached the Yarra and joined his party, beginning the journal's record of building, trading and quarrelling with Batman's men over who had the right to the riverbank. The sources differ on whether he arrived on 10 or 16 October.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878) gives 10 October; SLV early-history timeline gives 16 October

entries.headline: Despatch to London on the intrusion
entries.digest: Bourke sent his proclamation to Glenelg with a despatch describing the Association's settlement as an intrusion on part of the territory under his commission. He argued that the Crown should control settlement there rather than leave it to private bargains.
entries.quote: this intrusion upon part of the territory
entries.source_note: Bourke to Glenelg, 10 October 1835 (Despatch 99), in Labilliere (1878); Documenting a Democracy

entries.headline: Batman writes again to Arthur
entries.digest: Batman wrote again to Arthur from Launceston as the Association pressed its case after Bourke's proclamation. The Association continued to treat its deed as a just arrangement with the owners of the soil and went on delivering tribute goods.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878) lists the letter of 23 October 1835; Knapman (2022) on tribute deliveries to 1838

entries.headline: Gellibrand sails with sheep
entries.digest: Gellibrand embarked on the Norval with his son Tom and others, carrying sheep. A gale held the vessel for a week and over a hundred sheep died before they made land.
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 17–24 January 1836

entries.headline: Wedge's description goes to London
entries.digest: Arthur forwarded Wedge's description of the country around Port Phillip to the Colonial Office. Wedge's survey made the case for occupation; the Association hoped it would also strengthen its claim.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878)

entries.headline: Arriving on foot at Batman's settlement
entries.digest: After walking overland from Western Port, Gellibrand's party reached the mouth of the Yarra and came into the settlement about noon. Batman sent four Sydney men to look for the lost sheep.
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 31 January 1836

entries.headline: An offer to Buckley
entries.digest: Gellibrand talked with Buckley and offered him the post of superintendent over the Aboriginal people, to act as interpreter. He recorded Buckley's view that the people could only be moved by kindness and conciliation.
entries.quote: only be acted upon by kindness and conciliation
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 1 February 1836

entries.headline: Buckley meets his people again
entries.digest: On the Bellarine Peninsula the party met a group of three men, five women and about twelve children who knew Buckley. Gellibrand described their joy at seeing him and gave a blanket for Buckley's old friend, then presents to all before moving on.
entries.quote: tears of joy and delight running down their cheeks
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 5 February 1836

entries.headline: The interpreter among his kin
entries.digest: In Gellibrand's account Buckley was the go-between, greeted with tears by the families he had lived among. His position was double: he carried the Association's presents and messages while being bound to the people whose land the deed claimed.
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 5 February 1836

entries.headline: An assault, and a promise of removal
entries.digest: Gellibrand learned that a shepherd had assaulted an Aboriginal woman. Through Buckley he told the community that the offender would be sent away, and he gave the woman a red silk handkerchief. It is one of the few entries in which colonists record a wrong done and an answer owed under the new arrangement.
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 15 February 1836

entries.headline: Home with a favourable report
entries.digest: The vessel cleared the Heads at daylight and Gellibrand reached his Launceston hotel late at night. His closing notes praised the country as open and well watered and described its people as well made and intelligent.
entries.source_note: Gellibrand memoranda, 16–17 February 1836

entries.headline: London upholds Bourke
entries.digest: Glenelg told Bourke that he approved his course on the Port Phillip settlement. The Crown would not recognise the Association's title from the Aboriginal people; settlement at Port Phillip would proceed under government control.
entries.quote: I approve of the course which you have hitherto pursued
entries.source_note: Glenelg to Bourke, 13 April 1836, in Labilliere (1878)

entries.headline: The memoranda go to Bourke
entries.digest: Gellibrand sent his memoranda of the journey to Bourke, saying they were not an official document. Coming from the deed's lawyer, they put the Association's picture of peaceful dealings before the governor who had voided its deed.
entries.source_note: Gellibrand's covering letter, 18 April 1836 (Geelong Historical Society)

entries.headline: The rival journal ends
entries.digest: Fawkner's journal closes after a year that took the settlement from tents to a small township with a government officer on the way. By then the dispute was no longer between Batman and the Crown but between colonists over who would profit when the Crown sold the land.
entries.source_note: Fawkner journal ends 8 August 1836 (NLA MS 3224; Ray 1984)

entries.headline: The governor names Melbourne
entries.digest: Bourke visited Port Phillip, approved Robert Hoddle's town plan and named the settlement on the Yarra Melbourne, after the British prime minister. The village Batman had marked in June 1835 became a Crown town.
entries.source_note: La Trobe Society 'During this month: March'; SLV early-history timeline

entries.headline: Crown land sale on the Yarra
entries.digest: Melbourne's first Crown land sale was held under Bourke's government. The land Batman had claimed by deed was sold by the Crown, which had never recognised either his title or the Kulin's.
entries.source_note: Labilliere (1878)

claims.claim: Not making a treaty at first settlement was a great oversight; future land should be acquired by treaty
Terms agreed orally; goods (blankets, knives, tomahawks, scissors, looking-glasses, clothing, flour) handed over before the marks
Melbourne deed: about 500,000 acres granted in return for goods and a yearly 'rent or tribute'
Geelong deed: about 100,000 acres around Geelong and Indented Head on the same terms
Marks made, soil handed over, cloaks and weapons given: recorded only by Batman, no interpreter of Woiwurrung present
claims.evidence: Batman journal and deeds; Bischoff 2023; Attwood, eMelbourne

claims.claim: Position: the elders understood a tanderrum, granting access with obligations, not a sale
claims.evidence: Attwood (eMelbourne); Bischoff 2023; Wurundjeri Elder Uncle Andrew Gardiner (3KND, after 2021)

claims.claim: Position: the deed is a feoffment binding the grantees to a continuing tribute, not a purchase
A signing took place and he watched it as a boy, at a creek other than the one usually named
claims.evidence: Attwood (eMelbourne); History of St Albans 2025; recording date not established

claims.claim: Gumm authorised in writing to remove trespassers from the claimed land
About 600,000 acres bought from the chiefs, who marked boundary trees and gave soil; Crown recognition requested
Any bargain with Aboriginal people for land is void against the Crown; occupiers without authority are trespassers
The Association's settlement is an intrusion upon territory under his commission
A shepherd who assaulted an Aboriginal woman will be removed (told to the people through Buckley)
Bourke's course approved; no title from Aboriginal people recognised, settlement under Crown control
Position: there were no chiefs holding a superior right over the soil who could sell it
claims.evidence: Morgan, Life and Adventures of William Buckley (1852), via SLV ergo

claims.claim: The Association kept delivering tribute goods until 1838 despite the voiding

convergences.label: The deeds at the creek
convergences.note: Batman wrote the only same-day account; the ngurungaeta appear solely through his pen; Barak's memory of the day reached print decades later. A sale in one record, possibly a tanderrum in the other side's law, and a child's recollection of marks on paper.

convergences.label: Holding the claim while the map is drawn
convergences.note: Within a week Batman left men at Indented Head, Todd began his camp journal, and Wedge turned estimated distances into boundary lines at Kingston: the claim was being made real on paper and on the ground at once.

convergences.label: Buckley walks in
convergences.note: Todd's journal sees a huge stranger who has nearly lost his English; Buckley's memoir, told seventeen years later, recalls his own doubts about how he would be received.

convergences.label: Three days at the end of August
convergences.note: On 26 August Bourke voided the bargain in Sydney; on 28 August Arthur pardoned Buckley in Hobart; on 29–30 August Fawkner's party moored on the Yarra, where Wedge had been for three weeks. Neither governor could yet know what the other had done.

convergences.label: Despatch and arrival
convergences.note: As Bourke wrote to London of an intrusion, Fawkner (on 10 or 16 October) reached the settlement he meant to make his own: the Crown and the rival settler both rejected the deed for opposite purposes.

convergences.label: The lawyer on the ground
convergences.note: Days after Arthur sent Wedge's description to London, the deed's drafter walked the claimed land with Buckley as interpreter and recorded a reunion and an assault: the human relationships the deed's tribute clause assumed.

convergences.label: London's answer and Hobart's memoranda
convergences.note: Glenelg approved Bourke on 13 April; five days later, before the despatch could arrive, Gellibrand sent Bourke his picture of peaceful dealing. The decision had already been taken.

ties.note: Parties to the 6 June 1835 exchange; only Batman's account of it survives.
Barak was the son of Bebejan and nephew of Billibellary, both identified by later historians among the signatories.
Todd was Batman's employee and recorder, left at Indented Head on 9 June 1835.
Buckley walked into Todd's camp in July 1835; Todd recorded the meeting.
Wedge met Buckley in August 1835 and recommended his pardon.
Buckley interpreted for Gellibrand in February 1836.
Gellibrand drafted the deed Batman carried and became a trustee of the land conveyed on 30 June 1835.
Bourke's proclamation of 26 August 1835 voided the bargain on which Batman's claim rested.
Bourke's despatch of 10 October 1835 drew Glenelg's approval of 13 April 1836.
Rival founders of Melbourne; Fawkner rejected the deed and contested Batman's place for decades.
Both had been at the 1803 Sullivan Bay settlement, Fawkner as a boy with his convict father, Buckley as a convict who escaped from it.

threads_out.note: Bourke's 1835 doctrine that private purchases from Indigenous people were void against the Crown was applied in New Zealand: Gipps's January 1840 proclamation, read by Hobson at Kororāreka, refused to recognise land bought privately from Māori. Hobson's HMS Rattlesnake carried Bourke to Port Phillip in 1837.

In October 1834 the Quaker James Backhouse urged that Australian colonists follow William Penn's example of treaty before settlement; the Pennsylvania treaty tradition that Penn began is the setting of the Lancaster council of 1744.

The town Bourke named in 1837 was transformed by the Victorian gold rush from 1851, part of the wave of gold rushes that followed California's; the Port Phillip District became the colony of Victoria that same year.
